candidate.answerReason: Equal tangents give PQ=4+9=13. The endpoint separations parallel and perpendicular to the parallel tangents are 5 and 2r, respectively. Hence 25+4r²=169, so the positive radius is 6.

methods.label: Tangent lengths and a right triangle
methods.explanation:
The third tangent lets us find \(PQ\): tangent segments from the same external point have equal lengths. Thus
\[
PT''=PT=4,\qquad QT''=QT'=9.
\]
The figure places \(T''\) between \(P\) and \(Q\), so \(PQ=4+9=13\).

A radius to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent. Since the tangents at \(T\) and \(T'\) are distinct and parallel, their perpendicular radii lie on the same diameter. Consequently \(TT'=2r\).

Drop a perpendicular from \(P\) to the lower tangent, meeting it at \(H\). The quadrilateral \(TPHT'\) is a rectangle, so \(PH=TT'=2r\) and \(T'H=TP=4\). Since \(T'Q=9\), we have \(HQ=9-4=5\). Right triangle \(PHQ\) therefore gives
\[
(2r)^2+5^2=13^2,
\qquad 4r^2=144,
\qquad r^2=36.
\]
A radius is positive, so \(\boxed{r=6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: Equal tangents, perpendicular radii, rectangle properties, and the Pythagorean theorem give a complete elementary solution.

methods.label: Tangent angle bisectors and similarity
methods.explanation:
Joining the external points to the center reveals another useful feature: the center lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents from each point. Hence \(OP\) bisects \(\angle TPQ\), and \(OQ\) bisects \(\angle T'QP\).

Because \(PT\) and \(QT'\) are parallel rays pointing in the same direction, the angles they make with the opposite rays \(PQ\) and \(QP\) are supplementary. Therefore
\[
\angle OPQ+\angle OQP
=\frac12(180^\circ)=90^\circ.
\]
The angle sum in triangle \(POQ\) now gives \(\angle POQ=90^\circ\).

The radius \(OT''\) is perpendicular to the tangent \(PQ\). Thus it is the altitude from the right angle of triangle \(POQ\) to its hypotenuse. Write \(X=T''\). Equal tangent lengths give \(PX=4\), \(QX=9\), and \(OX=r\).

Right triangles \(PXO\) and \(OXQ\) are similar: both have a right angle at \(X\), and \(\angle XPO=\angle XOQ\), since each is complementary to \(\angle OQP\). Their corresponding sides give
\[
\frac{PX}{OX}=\frac{OX}{XQ},
\qquad \frac4r=\frac r9.
\]
Since \(r>0\), cross-multiplication is valid and gives \(r^2=36\). Therefore \(\boxed{r=6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: The alternative uses elementary angle bisection, parallel-line angles, and AA similarity to derive the altitude relation directly.

candidate.annotationRationale: Both routes depend on tangent-radius perpendicularity and the equal-tangent theorem, making those the route-neutral targets. Segment arithmetic, circle terminology, and selecting a positive square root support both methods. The first route adds rectangle properties and Pythagoras; the second uses the angle-bisector part of the tangent theorem, parallel-line angles, and similar-triangle ratios. The alternatives remain separate and do not imply that every learner must demonstrate both.

review.mathematicalCheck: The figure confirms that T'' lies between P and Q and that both endpoints lie on the same side of the tangency diameter. Equal tangents give PQ=13; the rectangular construction gives perpendicular separation 2r and horizontal separation 5, so 4r²+25=169 and r=6. Independently, tangent angle bisectors make POQ a right triangle, and the stated AA similarity correctly yields 4/r=r/9. Positivity selects the unique radius 6.
review.levelCheck: Both explanations use elementary circle geometry and school-level triangle reasoning. The similarity method derives its altitude relation explicitly and introduces no advanced shortcut.
